festivals.name: BlackStar Film Festival
festivals.fit_reason: The single best-fit festival in the Black-cinema lane: BlackStar exists precisely for visionary work by Black/Brown/Indigenous directors, and consistently programs diaspora spirituality, ancestral memory, and formally bold craft — a chiaroscuro Yoruba-faith period short by a Nigerian director is dead center. Oscar-qualifying (Short Narrative jury award, confirmed on the Academy's 98th and 99th lists) AND BAFTA-qualifying, with the theatrical-run requirement waived for winners. Premiere status is 'preferred' but not required, so it slots into a strategy after a bigger world premiere. Student fees are waived with valid enrollment — an AFI thesis film may submit free.

findings.topic: Q1 — Do shorts hire publicists, and when is it worth it?
findings.summary: Most shorts do NOT hire a publicist — even Sundance's own in-house publicist says short filmmakers usually rely on the festival's press office, which pitches press on the film's behalf. Hiring one becomes rational only in two situations: a world premiere at a top-tier festival (Sundance/SXSW/Tribeca) where the director has a concrete career objective (representation, feature financing), or a later Oscar-qualification/awards campaign. Never hire before you have an acceptance in hand.
findings.detail: Sundance publicist Susan Szotyori (No Film School Q&A): 'For short films, filmmakers oftentimes opt not to hire a publicist' — the festival's in-house publicity team then pitches press, connects filmmakers with journalists, and handles interview logistics; she calls DIY campaigns 'often successful' for shorts, while recommending publicists for features. The Film Collaborative's festival-PR guide is blunt: 'Don't hire a publicist if you haven't gotten into a film festival or have a theatrical/digital release' — you get no return if the film isn't screening. K2 Publicity (via No Film School) frames the trigger as 'world premiering at a major or specialty festival.' For a 13-minute AFI thesis short, the practical read (inference, consistent across sources): skip paid PR for regional/mid-tier premieres; consider it only for a Sundance/SXSW/Tribeca premiere or an Oscar-shortlist push, and treat the director-as-emerging-talent story (Nigerian director, Yoruba spiritual drama, AFI thesis) as the pitchable angle, since publicists say angle-finding is their core value (Film Festival Secrets / Bright Iris).

findings.topic: Q2 — Real cost numbers: festival PR packages and retainers
findings.summary: Festival publicity is usually flat-fee, not retainer: roughly $7K–12K for a major festival (Sundance/TIFF/Cannes/SXSW) and $3K–7K for regional or locally-based festivals (LA, AFI FEST, New York, Tribeca), per The Film Collaborative. Boutique indie-film publicists start around $5K per campaign; monthly retainers run $3K–20K at the extremes. Shorts-specific awards campaigns run from a few thousand dollars (Academy mailshots) to $5K–10K typical, up to $100K+ comprehensive; a full Oscar-shorts push with top firms implies $10K–15K/month PR retainers.
findings.detail: The Film Collaborative (festival PR budgeting): major festivals '$7-12K' because publicists cover their own travel/lodging; regional festivals '$3-7K' using locally-based publicists; festival campaigns are flat-fee. AMW's film-PR pricing guide: boutique indie specialists start ~$5,000; monthly retainers $3K–$20K (top end is celebrity publicists); notes most film publicists charge project fees, and typical indie marketing spend overall is $2,500–$7,500. For shorts specifically, Screen Daily's shorts-campaign feature (quoting London Flair's Catherine Lyn Scott and See-Through Films' Kathleen McInnis): minimal campaigns are 'a few thousand dollars' for Academy mailshots, typical $5,000–$10,000, comprehensive up to $100,000. The Rough Cut newsletter's Oscar-shorts breakdown puts a full modern campaign at $150K–$300K: PR retainers $60K–90K over ~6 months, Academy Screening Room fees $12.5K–20K, trade ads ~$50K, voter events $20K–50K, with success bonuses ($15K–25K for a nomination, $20K–50K for a win) — and notes no individual filmmakers self-fund at that scale (funders are streamers, boutique distributors, or EP-credit buyers). Caveat: the $3K–12K festival figures were written for features; no published shorts-specific festival flat fee surfaced — shorts either pay in the same low band, share a publicist across a shorts block, or use the festival press office (inference from the Sundance Q&A and Screen Daily block-screening cost-splitting practice).

findings.topic: Q3 — What a festival publicist actually does for a short at Sundance/SXSW/Tribeca
findings.summary: Deliverables are: press-material prep and angle development, targeted pitching to press attending the festival, interview scheduling and press-line staffing at the premiere, screener management, and coverage tracking — with the honest expectation that shorts rarely get trade reviews, so the win condition is director profiles, 'shorts to watch' roundups, and craft/interview pieces rather than Variety/Deadline reviews. Several strategically placed articles beat one big-name outlet.
findings.detail: From the Sundance publicist Q&A: publicists gather stills/posters/trailers/press kits, coordinate press access, staff premiere press lines with photo and interview ops, pitch outlets, and assemble coverage; smaller films' publicists often work remotely or attend only opening days when press density peaks. Sundance's shorts-programmer advice: a good publicist 'will help manage expectations' and knows 'several strategically placed articles are often more valuable than one piece in a big name outlet.' The Film Collaborative adds: strategic plan, knowing which press are attending, screener distribution, coordination with sales agents. Reality check on trade coverage for shorts — See-Through Films' Kathleen McInnis: 'Getting press coverage for shorts in phase one is next to impossible unless you have a celebrity attachment.' Filmmaker Magazine's 25 New Faces list — the single most career-relevant press placement for an emerging director — explicitly positions itself as 'a genuine place for discovery' and NOT 'another publicist-driven list,' so it is earned by the work and festival visibility, not bought. Online-premiere placement (Vimeo Staff Pick Premiere, Short of the Week, a Vulture/NYT Op-Docs-style outlet for docs) is typically brokered after the festival run, and publicists or the filmmaker can pitch it directly (see Q5).

findings.topic: Q5 — Timing of hiring, and the DIY path if you skip PR
findings.summary: Hire within 1–2 months of the festival screening, never before acceptance — for Sundance that means the window opens with the late-Nov/early-Dec acceptance call, so press materials must exist BEFORE you're accepted. The DIY substitute is: a complete EPK built now, the festival's own press office as your pitch channel during the run, and the shorts-native online ecosystem (Short of the Week, Vimeo Staff Pick Premieres, Omeleto, Directors Notes) as the post-run distribution/press engine.
findings.detail: Timing (The Film Collaborative): budget for publicity at planning stage, but 'hire your publicist within 1-2 months of your festival screening' and 'create your press materials early.' DIY channel one — the EPK, standard components per Storydoc/Film Festival Secrets/Raindance guides: cover page with title/runtime/contacts, logline plus short/medium/long synopses (festivals and journalists lift these verbatim), director's statement, key cast/crew bios with headshots, 10–15 images mixing film stills and behind-the-scenes, technical specs (2.39:1, formats), full credits, laurels/awards list, trailer, and social links. DIY channel two — the festival press office: The Film Collaborative notes festival PR staff will 'point you towards journalists they think might be interested in your film' and give strategic guidance free. DIY channel three — post-run online premiere: Vimeo runs one Staff Pick Premiere per week with on- and off-platform editorial and marketing support; Vimeo's curators say they source shorts from Short of the Week, Directors Notes, Booooooom, and Nowness, so coverage on those sites feeds Staff Pick selection. In a Vimeo survey of Staff-Picked creators, 85% said it increased brand awareness, 68% said it led to paid/funded work, 61% said it helped launch their careers. Omeleto (large YouTube shorts channel) and Directors Notes (interview-led coverage) are the other standard post-run homes. Critical sequencing caveat for KILLER OF MEN: any public online release ends premiere eligibility at many festivals, so the online-premiere step belongs at the END of the 2026–2027 festival run, not before (Medium/CUT-UP on premiere status; consistent with the film's intact premiere status).

findings.topic: Q6 — PR for a craft-forward film chasing below-the-line/cinematography attention
findings.summary: The cinematography-community track is not publicist-driven at all — it runs through the ASC's own institutions: the ASC Student Heritage Awards (FilmFreeway entry; eligible if the DP graduates in 2026 or graduated in 2025 — squarely covers an AFI thesis DP), American Cinematographer's annual Rising Stars of Cinematography list, and AFI's own Cinematography Spotlight. Precedent is exact: AFI 2024 grad Zach Morrison won the ASC Student Heritage Award for a chiaroscuro-adjacent 1690s period short and was interviewed in American Cinematographer.
findings.detail: Channels, in order of leverage for this film: (1) ASC Student Heritage Awards — entries for the 2026 edition are open (theasc.com news + FilmFreeway page); eligibility requires the entrant to be sole cinematographer and to be graduating in 2026 or have graduated within the past year, judged by an ASC blue-ribbon panel; winners get theasc.com coverage and an awards ceremony alongside working ASC members. Zach Morrison (AFI class of 2024) won for 'The Witch Pricker and the Hair,' a 1690s Scotland period piece — a single-source-lighting period short from AFI winning this exact award is the strongest possible comp for KILLER OF MEN's DP. (2) American Cinematographer's 'Rising Stars of Cinematography' — annual editorial feature (2025 and 2026 editions confirmed on theasc.com) spotlighting ~9 emerging DPs, many with shorts-only credits; this is pitched/nominated editorial, not paid PR. (3) AFI Conservatory's Cinematography Spotlight — AFI's own showcase page for each graduating cinematography class (2026 edition live, 25 DPs with reels/contacts), i.e., an in-house channel the film's DP should already be in. Strategic difference from normal festival PR (labeled inference, but well-supported): for a craft calling-card film, the DP is a second, separate press surface — the DP pitches ASC/American Cinematographer and cinematography outlets with lighting breakdowns (single-source firelight, 2.39:1 tenebrism) while the director works the festival/identity/story angle — and none of the ASC-side channels charge PR fees; they are awards entries and editorial pitches. American Cinematographer's remit explicitly includes short films alongside features/TV/music videos (Muck Rack outlet profile).

findings.topic: Extra — BAFTA vs Oscar campaign rules for shorts, and who funds big campaigns
findings.summary: If the film qualifies for awards later, the rulebooks diverge sharply: BAFTA prohibits 'campaigning of any kind' in shorts categories (press only, publicist disclosure required), while the Academy permits broader promotion in later phases — and official Academy channels (member email blasts, Academy Screening Room) are the cost-effective backbone. Six-figure shorts campaigns are funded by streamers, distributors, or EP-credit buyers, never by the filmmaker.
findings.detail: Screen Daily: London Flair's Catherine Lyn Scott on shorts campaigning — 'You can't campaign, you can't talk to voters, you can't do anything other than press'; Academy email blasts to relevant branches are 'well worth doing'; in-person screenings with Q&As beat online-only, and block screenings split costs among multiple shorts; studio campus screenings (Pixar, Disney, Netflix) in Sept–Nov reach likely voters. Rough Cut: Academy Screening Room fees $12.5K–20K plus ~$5K watermarking are near-mandatory infrastructure for a serious Oscar-shorts run; the realistic funders are streamers (Netflix, The New Yorker), boutique shorts distributors, studios, or high-net-worth individuals buying EP credits. Practical implication for an AFI thesis film (inference): the cheap, legitimate awards moves — qualifying via festival wins, Academy member mailshots, block screenings — cost a few thousand dollars; anything beyond that needs a distribution partner, which is itself a reason the post-festival online-premiere decision (Q5) should wait until the awards picture is clear.

findings.topic: Extra — The realistic PR playbook for KILLER OF MEN (synthesis)
findings.summary: Synthesis of the sourced findings into a decision rule: build the full EPK now (pre-acceptance), spend $0 on PR below the top festival tier and use each festival's press office, hold a $3K–7K flat-fee boutique publicist (from the Sundance list's shorts-tagged firms, or See-Through Films for strategy) in reserve for a Sundance/SXSW/Tribeca-tier world premiere, run the DP's ASC/American Cinematographer track in parallel for free, and save the online premiere (Short of the Week / Vimeo Staff Pick / Omeleto) for the end of the run.
findings.detail: This is labeled inference — a strategy assembled from the evidence, not a claim found in any single source. The load-bearing facts behind it: shorts usually skip publicists and festival press offices pitch for them (Sundance in-house publicist); paid festival PR only pays off at premiere moments ($3K–7K regional / $7K–12K major, flat-fee, hired 1–2 months out — The Film Collaborative); the highest-value emerging-director press (Filmmaker's 25 New Faces) is explicitly not publicist-accessible; the cinematography channels (ASC Student Heritage Awards with a direct AFI period-short precedent, AC Rising Stars) are free entries/pitches with a hard 2026 eligibility window that matches this film's January 2026 completion; and the online platforms that end premiere eligibility also deliver the career payoff (85%/68%/61% Staff Pick survey numbers), so they are sequenced last. One deadline-sensitive note: the ASC Student Heritage Awards 2026 entry window is open now per theasc.com — the DP eligibility clock (graduating 2026 or graduated 2025) makes this the single most time-sensitive item in the whole PR lane.

findings.topic: Q1 — What world / international / North American / US premiere actually mean
findings.summary: There is no industry-wide statute; each festival defines premiere tiers in its own regulations, but the definitions converge. TIFF 2026 and the Berlinale FAQ publish the cleanest canonical definitions, and both hinge on the concept of a PUBLIC screening — private showings do not count.
findings.detail: TIFF 2026 Submissions FAQ (official PDF, verbatim): World Premiere = 'The Film has not had and will not have any public screening anywhere in the world before its scheduled presentation at the Festival.' International Premiere = 'The Film has only had a public screening in its country of origin (if the country of origin is not in North America)... (Please note: If a United States Film had a public screening only in the United States, it would qualify as an International Premiere.)' North American Premiere = public screenings in other countries but none yet in Canada or the US (Mexico/Caribbean screenings do not affect it). Canadian Premiere = screened elsewhere incl. the US, but never in Canada. Berlinale FAQ (2026 cycle): World premiere = 'The film has never been shown anywhere publicly.' International premiere = 'The film has only been released theatrically or presented at a festival in its country of origin, but nowhere else.' European premiere = shown outside Europe but never in Europe. 'US premiere' (used by US fests like Tribeca) = never publicly screened in the United States. Key mechanic: a 'public screening' at TIFF is one that was 'advertised and/or ticketed' with public and/or press attending — the definition every other question turns on. Note the useful TIFF quirk for a US film like Killer of Men: US-only festival screenings still leave it an 'International Premiere' in TIFF's system, so a small US premiere does not disqualify it from TIFF.

findings.topic: Q2 — What each major festival actually REQUIRES for shorts (current regulations, cited)
findings.summary: The split is stark: the European A-list (Cannes all three sections, Berlinale, Venice) hard-requires world/international premieres for shorts, and TIFF requires at least a North American premiere at submission. Sundance, Clermont-Ferrand, SXSW, Tribeca, Palm Springs, Aspen, BlackStar, HollyShorts and Telluride require NO premiere for shorts — most merely prefer one.
findings.detail: SUNDANCE 2027 (official Rules PDF, dated June 2026, verbatim for U.S. Short Films): 'Projects completed after December 31, 2025 are still eligible to submit to the Festival, regardless of premiere status.' Only shorts made public before Jan 1, 2026 are barred. NO premiere requirement whatsoever. Shorts = under 50 min. Deadlines: early Jul 13 / official Aug 3 / late Aug 31, 2026. — CANNES 2026 regs, Short Films in Competition (official page): must 'not have been presented in another international film festival', 'not have been screened elsewhere than their home country', 'not have been screened on the Internet', made in the 12 months preceding the festival, MAX 15 MINUTES including credits (13-min film fits). — SEMAINE DE LA CRITIQUE 2026 regs (official): foreign shorts 'must not have participated in any festival outside its country of origin... or film event (excluding film markets)'; 'must not have been shown on the Internet or broadcasted on TV, or commercially released, including in its country of origin'; completed within 12 months prior to the festival; ≤59 min. — DIRECTORS' FORTNIGHT (Quinzaine) 2026 (official FAQ): outside country of origin, no prior international festival/film event; not shown on Internet/TV/commercially released in France; made within 12 months preceding; shorts <60 min. — BERLINALE SHORTS (official regs page, fetched in full): world or international premieres only, world prioritized; never shown publicly outside country of origin, never publicly in Germany; 'have neither been broadcast on television nor presented on the internet/VOD'; completed within 12 months prior to festival start; ≤30 min. — VENICE 83rd (2026) (Biennale official): 'Only works presented as world premieres are eligible' for Orizzonti incl. Orizzonti Corti (shorts ≤20 min); no public or press screening, no prior festival, no internet streaming; completed after Sept 6, 2025; deadline was May 28, 2026. — TIFF 2026 (official FAQ/Eligibility PDFs): 'Upon submission, Films must have a World, International or North American premiere status' (Canadian premiere at TIFF's discretion); shorts ≤40 min; completed on/after Sept 4, 2025. — TELLURIDE (official film_entry page, 2026): North American premiere effectively required for features only; 'not so strict about shorts' — but does not accept shorts already released online. Not an Oscar-qualifying fest for shorts. — SXSW (official support article, corroborated): premiere status is 'an important factor in programming decisions rather than an absolute eligibility condition'; previously screened shorts considered if not extensively exposed. 2027: completed 2025–early 2027, ≤40 min. — TRIBECA (FilmFreeway listing, 2026 cycle): no premiere required to submit, but 'entries must be at least a U.S. Premiere to be eligible for awards'; W/I/NA/US premieres 'may be given priority'; shorts ≤39:59; 2026 rule barred projects made publicly available before May 1, 2026 (2027 rules expected to roll the date). — CLERMONT-FERRAND 49th (2027) (official lecourt-clermont.org): 'does not require exclusivity or a premiere'; films already at festivals or online ARE eligible; International Competition ≤40 min; films completed in 2026 → deadline Sept 24, 2026; festival Jan 29–Feb 6, 2027. — PALM SPRINGS SHORTFEST (2027 cycle, FilmFreeway summary): completed 2026 or 2027, ≤40 min, no premiere required; BUT films already on internet/national broadcast are shunted to the 'Online Film Festival' category only (out of the main Oscar-qualifying competition). — ASPEN SHORTSFEST 36th (2027): premieres 'prioritized' (W/I/NA/US), not required; entries cannot have premiered before March 2026 (per 2027 call summary — verify on FilmFreeway); films publicly broadcast/online in the U.S. ineligible; restricted online-festival screenings OK; ≤40 min; DCP-only. — BLACKSTAR (2026 official submissions page): premiere 'not required for eligibility, preference is given to premiere status films' (Philadelphia/East Coast/US/NA/World); director must identify as Black, Brown and/or Indigenous (fits the director); shorts ≤40 min. — HOLLYSHORTS (FilmFreeway/Festhome): no premiere requirement stated in rules; ≤40 min; Oscar-qualifying in 4 categories.

findings.topic: Q3 — Do school showcases, cast-and-crew screenings, or WIP screenings break premiere status?
findings.summary: Cast-and-crew, friends-and-family, and NDA'd private screenings do NOT break premiere status anywhere — TIFF says so explicitly and every definition keys off 'public screening'. School showcases are a gray zone: TIFF explicitly carves out 'compulsory school showcases', but Venice/Cannes/Berlinale's 'never shown publicly' language means a ticketed, advertised, open-to-the-public AFI showcase could technically void a world premiere there.
findings.detail: TIFF 2026 FAQ, verbatim: 'TIFF considers a public screening to be a screening where the public and/or press attended and the screening was advertised and/or ticketed. Exceptions include a screening where the public attended, but there was a non-disclosure agreement and no advertising, and/or a private friends-and-family/cast-and-crew screening. There may also be exclusions for compulsory school showcases. Please contact submissions@tiff.net if you are uncertain.' Sundance 2027 Rules (features language, showing the same principle): films 'exhibited theatrically at one or more private screenings for which tickets were or will not be made available to the general public retain eligibility'; WIP screenings 'at either public or private events' retain eligibility for incomplete versions (and a publicly ticketed WIP only disqualifies if the final version isn't significantly different) — and for shorts none of this even matters since Sundance shorts have no premiere requirement at all. The strict end: Venice requires the film 'must not have had any public or press screening'; Berlinale world premiere = 'never been shown anywhere publicly'; Cannes = 'not have been screened elsewhere than their home country' (a US school screening is in-country, so Cannes official-competition eligibility survives a domestic showcase — but Berlinale/Venice world-premiere STATUS would not if the showcase was public). PRACTICAL GUIDANCE for the AFI thesis showcase: if it is invitation/industry/NDA-style or a compulsory curricular screening, premiere status survives everywhere; if it is publicly ticketed and advertised (some AFI showcase nights are), treat the film as having had a US public screening — which still leaves TIFF (International Premiere), Cannes official competition (in-country screening allowed), and every no-premiere-required festival intact, but kills a Venice/Berlinale world premiere claim. Inference labeled as such: festivals almost never police unadvertised school screenings, but the safe play is to email the specific festival before claiming World Premiere. This determination matters most for Venice/Berlinale, which are likely off the table anyway on completion-window grounds (see the completion-window finding).

findings.topic: Q4 — Online availability: trailer vs full film vs password-protected Vimeo
findings.summary: Universal pattern across every festival checked: trailers and clips are always fine, password-protected private links are always fine, but a PUBLICLY viewable full film online is fatal at Cannes/Berlinale/Venice, geoblock-dependent at TIFF, category-killing at Palm Springs and Aspen, and irrelevant at Sundance (for recent shorts), Clermont, and HollyShorts.
findings.detail: Berlinale FAQ, verbatim: 'If the film was available on the internet or on VOD, it is no longer eligible... Sole exceptions are personal, password-restricted links, which were created for a festival submission process.' And: 'A trailer does not present any breach of our regulations.' This trailer/password-link doctrine is echoed everywhere — TIFF FAQ: 'Posting a trailer, clip, and/or actor reel online from your Film does not disqualify your Film,' and Tribeca/SXSW/TIFF all REQUIRE a password-protected streaming link as the submission format, so a private Vimeo screener never breaks anything. Full-film public availability by festival: Cannes (all 3 shorts sections): ineligible ('must not have been screened on the Internet'). Berlinale: ineligible, including prior online-festival streaming. Venice: ineligible ('must not have had any form of commercial distribution or streaming on the Internet'). TIFF: ineligible only if publicly viewable IN North America — 'Films that are publicly posted or exhibited online but geoblocked to a region outside of North America are still eligible.' Telluride: does not accept shorts released online. Aspen: 'Films publicly broadcast or made available online in the U.S. are ineligible,' though geo-restricted online-festival screenings are excused. Palm Springs ShortFest: previously-online films are relegated to the non-competitive 'Online Film Festival' category. SXSW: prior online release forfeits World Premiere labeling and is weighed in programming, but is not an absolute bar for shorts. Sundance 2027: a short completed after Dec 31, 2025 is eligible even if it is sitting on YouTube ('regardless of premiere status'; only pre-Jan-1-2026 public availability disqualifies). Clermont-Ferrand and HollyShorts: online availability is a non-issue. Sector-wide data (Stephen Follows, 10,549 festivals): only 11.1% of festivals actively reject already-online films; 16% explicitly accept them; 72.8% are silent. ACADEMY interplay: winning a designated festival award qualifies a short for the Oscar 'regardless of any prior public exhibition or distribution by nontheatrical means' (Rule 17 II.A.2) — online release never blocks the festival route; it only blocks the theatrical route (II.B, 15%-of-runtime allowance). BOTTOM LINE for this film: keep the full film off the public internet until the European-premiere question and the Oscar-qualifying run are resolved; trailer and password-protected screeners are safe everywhere.

findings.topic: Q5 — Does a small-festival premiere kill your chances at the big ones? (practical, not just rules)
findings.summary: By rule, a small US premiere kills exactly three doors for a US short: Berlinale, Venice, and (if it toured internationally) Cannes — everything else on the US shorts circuit stays open, including TIFF. Practically, programmers at premiere-proud festivals (SXSW, Tribeca, Aspen, BlackStar) do weigh freshness, but a low-profile regional premiere rarely sinks a strong short; 'extensive exposure' is the phrase SXSW itself uses as the real threshold.
findings.detail: What the rules say: Sundance shorts — zero premiere requirement (any number of prior festivals explicitly allowed); Clermont — 'special attention will be paid to films that have not yet been shown' but no requirement; SXSW — 'premiere status is an important factor in programming decisions,' and previously screened films are still considered 'if programmers strongly connect with the film and it has not already received extensive exposure'; TIFF — 'The Film's premiere status will be taken into consideration when final programming decisions are made,' but a US-only-screened US film still holds International Premiere status and remains fully eligible; Tribeca — priority to premieres, and a US premiere is needed for AWARDS (so any prior US festival screening removes the film from Tribeca's Oscar-qualifying award pool — a real cost); Aspen/BlackStar — stated preference/priority for premieres. Evidence-based practical read (labeled inference, consistent with programmer commentary and the Follows data): (a) the world-premiere card is worth the most at Sundance/SXSW even though neither requires it — programmers like announcing premieres and press coverage clusters on them; (b) a single small-festival premiere mostly costs marketing language, not eligibility — the killer is accumulation ('extensive exposure') and online release, not the first screening; (c) the asymmetric, irreversible losses are the European A-list (Berlinale/Venice: any prior public screening outside — or for world-premiere status, anywhere — ends it) and Tribeca's award track (any prior US screening); (d) therefore the standard calculus for a US short with Sundance-caliber craft: hold everything until the Sundance 2027 decision (submitted by Aug 31, 2026; decisions early-mid December 2026), because holding costs nothing — every other target festival's 2027 deadline (Clermont Sept 24, 2026 excepted) falls after Sundance notifications. Clermont is the one pre-decision conflict, and Clermont itself doesn't care about premieres, so submitting there in parallel is riskless to Clermont and only relevant if selected AND the team still wants a Berlinale/Venice world premiere (already implausible on completion windows).

findings.topic: Q6 — Academy Live Action Short qualification: windows, routes, and when to choose (with a numbering correction)
findings.summary: Correction to the brief: the 2027 ceremony is the 99th Academy Awards (March 14, 2027; shorts qualifying window Oct 1, 2025–Sept 30, 2026) and the 2028 ceremony is the 100th (March 5, 2028; shorts window Oct 1, 2026–Sept 30, 2027, estimated from the fixed annual pattern). Three routes: qualifying festival award, 7-day theatrical run in one of six metros (barred to student films), or a Student Academy Award medal — and a film must be submitted in the same awards year it qualifies, within two years of completion.
findings.detail: Ceremony dates (Academy/ABC announcement, April 2026): '99th Oscars will take place Sunday, March 14, 2027, and the 100th Oscars will take place Sunday, March 5, 2028.' SHORTS ELIGIBILITY WINDOWS (distinct from the features' calendar-year window): official 99th Shorts Qualifying Festival List header, verbatim: 'Films that win a qualifying festival award between October 1, 2025, and September 30, 2026, may be eligible to submit for 99th Academy Awards consideration.' 99th submission deadlines: qualify Oct 1, 2025–Jun 30, 2026 → materials due 5pm PT Aug 13, 2026; qualify Jul 1–Sep 30, 2026 → due Oct 8, 2026. 100th window: Oct 1, 2026–Sept 30, 2027 (estimated from the unbroken Oct 1–Sept 30 pattern; the 100th list is not yet published). 101st window would be Oct 1, 2027–Sept 30, 2028 (same pattern) — but see the two-year rule below for why it's out of reach. THE THREE ROUTES (Rule Seventeen, 98th AA official text, full PDF retrieved): (1) FESTIVAL: 'won a qualifying award at a competitive film festival, as specified in the Short Film Qualifying Festival List, regardless of any prior public exhibition or distribution by nontheatrical means' — it must be the exact designated award, not mere selection. Designated qualifying awards at the target festivals (from the official 99th list): Sundance (Short Film Grand Jury Prize + 4 jury awards incl. US Fiction), Cannes (Short Film Palme d'Or only), Berlinale (Golden Bear for Best Short Film), Venice (Orizzonti Award for Best Short Film), TIFF (Best International/Canadian Short Film), SXSW (Narrative Shorts Jury Award), Tribeca (Best Narrative Short), Clermont-Ferrand (Grand Prix International + National), Palm Springs ShortFest (Best of Fest, Best Live Action ≤15 min, Best Live Action >15 min), Aspen (Best Drama, Best Comedy, Best Short Short, etc.), BlackStar (Short Narrative Jury Award), HollyShorts (Grand Prize + Best Live Action + 2 more), AFI FEST (Grand Jury Prize – Live Action Short). Telluride is NOT on the shorts qualifying list. (2) THEATRICAL: paid-admission run of 'at least seven consecutive days in the same commercial motion picture theater,' screenings at least once daily, advertised, in one of six metros — Los Angeles County; NYC five boroughs; Bay Area; Chicago/Cook County; Dallas-Fort Worth; Atlanta/Fulton County — via 35mm/70mm or SMPTE DCP (Blu-ray insufficient). Critical for a thesis film, verbatim: 'Student films cannot qualify with a theatrical release.' Theatrical-route films also must not have ANY nontheatrical public exhibition (TV/VOD/internet) before the qualifying run (15%-of-runtime allowance); festival and SAA routes are exempt from that rule. (3) STUDENT ACADEMY AWARDS: 'won a Gold, Silver or Bronze Medal award in the Academy's [year] Student Academy Awards competition in the Narrative or Alternative/Experimental categories' — the natural extra route for an AFI Conservatory thesis (2027 SAA cycle rules on oscars.org; the site blocks automated retrieval, so the SAA entry window for 2027 is unverified — have the team check oscars.org/saa directly). WHEN THE FILM MUST CHOOSE: Rule 17 III.I, verbatim: 'No short film may be submitted more than once for Academy Awards consideration. A short film must be submitted in the same Awards year in which it qualifies,' and qualification 'must take place within two years of the film's completion date.' Picture-locked January 2026 → the film must qualify by roughly January 2028, i.e., in the 99th window (award won by Sept 30, 2026 — only HollyShorts Aug 2026 / BlackStar Aug 2026-type wins could have done this; that window is now nearly closed) or, realistically, the 100th window (Oct 1, 2026–Sept 30, 2027): a qualifying-award win anywhere from Sundance Jan 2027 through HollyShorts/BlackStar Aug 2027 lands the film in the 100th Oscars race (March 2028 ceremony), with submission materials due ~mid-August 2027 or early October 2027 by pattern. Practical reading (labeled inference, consistent with standard awards practice): winning a qualifying award obliges the choice that same cycle — you cannot bank a Sundance 2027 win for the 101st Oscars; skipping a cycle means gambling on winning a NEW qualifying award in the next window before the two-years-from-completion clock (≈Jan 2028) expires, which the 101st window (starting Oct 2027) barely and riskily permits.

findings.summary: A January-2026-completed film has quietly aged out of most 2027 A-list world-premiere sections, which all require completion within ~12 months of the festival — but it fits Sundance 2027 exactly, and Sundance's late deadline is August 31, 2026, six days from today (Aug 25, 2026).
findings.detail: Completion windows against a Jan-2026 picture-lock: CANNES 2027 (all three shorts sections, May 2027): films must be 'made in the twelve months preceding' the festival → cutoff ≈ May 2026 → INELIGIBLE on completion date (unless the team can credibly date completion to final deliverables later in 2026 — grading was January 2026, so this is a stretch; La Cinef, Cannes' student section, is the one Cannes door with different rules worth checking at festival-cannes.com/la-cinef). VENICE 2027 (84th, Sept 2027): 83rd required completion after Sept 6, 2025; pattern rolls to ≈ Sept 2026 for the 84th → INELIGIBLE (estimated from 2026 pattern). TIFF 2027 (Sept 2027): 2026 edition required completion on/after Sept 4, 2025; pattern rolls to ≈ Sept 2026 → likely INELIGIBLE (estimated from 2026 pattern; TIFF 2026's deadline May 8, 2026 already passed). THE ONES THAT FIT: SUNDANCE 2027 (Jan 22–Feb 1, 2027 per Sundance announcements): eligibility = completed after Dec 31, 2025 → a Jan-2026 film is EXACTLY the intended cohort; late deadline Mon Aug 31, 2026 ($95) — six days away; this is the single most urgent action item in the whole premiere strategy. Net strategic consequence: the classic 'hold everything for a European world premiere' play is mostly moot for this film — the realistic premiere crown jewels are Sundance 2027 (no premiere required but the World Premiere laurel is available), then the US Oscar-qualifying shorts circuit (Clermont/Aspen/ShortFest/Tribeca/BlackStar/HollyShorts/AFI FEST) through the 100th-Oscars qualifying window ending Sept 30, 2027.

findings.topic: 1. Tiered-wave submission strategy and premiere-status sequencing
findings.summary: The standard playbook is three waves over ~18 months: 3-6 months of world-premiere attempts at top-tier festivals, then a cascade to Oscar-qualifying mid-tiers and identity/regional fits, then reassess. Critically for shorts, premiere status matters less than folklore says: Sundance accepts shorts that have screened anywhere including online, while Berlinale Shorts and some European A-listers still demand premieres — so the thing to actually protect is the ONLINE release, not every prior screening.
findings.detail: Wave structure (filmfestivalfever.substack.com, a working programmer's newsletter): Phase 1 (months 1-3 of the campaign) = only selective prestige festivals where world premieres matter (Sundance, Cannes, Berlinale, Venice, TIFF, SXSW, Tribeca — acceptance rates 1-4%, described bluntly as treating unsolicited entries as 'revenue-generating fodder'); Phase 2 (months 3-6) = expand to regional, thematic, and identity-fit festivals while staying selective; Phase 3 (6+ months of rejections) = reassess fit. ShowRunHer and Indie Shorts Mag frame the same thing as a reach/realistic/safety tiered list mapped 9-12 months ahead of target festival dates. The conventional premiere hold: keep the film off all public platforms while the top tier is in play; Miralot's guide phrases it as protecting premiere status 'like it's money in the bank.' The practical 12-month top-tier loop: Sundance shorts deadline falls in Aug-Sep for the January festival, Cannes in winter for May, Venice/TIFF in spring for fall — one calendar year covers every major once. KEY NUANCE for a short (verified via Short of the Week's festival-eligibility survey): ~64% of top festivals accept films already online; Sundance's shorts rules explicitly allow prior festival screenings, TV, and internet exhibition; BFI London deprioritizes but doesn't exclude non-premieres; Berlinale rejects online films from Competition/Berlinale Shorts (accepts in Panorama/Forum/Generation); DOK Leipzig excludes anything published online. So the real discipline is: (a) never release online until the run is over, (b) hold the WORLD premiere for the top tier for 6-12 months, (c) after the premiere lands, screenings at mid-tier fests cost almost nothing strategically — cascade freely.

findings.topic: 2. Real submission-budget numbers for a serious shorts campaign
findings.summary: Average short-film entry fee is $30-55 depending on deadline tier (Stephen Follows' Sept 2025 study of 4,631 festivals). A focused serious run is 15-20 festivals at $1,000-2,000 in fees, $3,000-5,000+ all-in with deliverables and travel; a saturation campaign runs to $10,000. Several elite festivals are free to enter (Cannes shorts, Clermont-Ferrand, Oberhausen), which stretches the budget at the very top.
findings.detail: Stephen Follows (September 2025, dataset of 4,631 festivals, fees normalized to USD): shorts average $30-55 across deadline tiers vs $47-87 for features; four standard deadline tiers (early/regular/late/final) with early-bird saving $20-40 per entry; fees over $100 for a short flagged as exploitative. Aggregate campaign numbers from multiple 2025-26 guides (CMS Productions, Future Film Academy, Beverly Boy): focus on 15-20 carefully selected festivals ≈ $1,000-2,000 in fees alone; $3,000-5,000+ total once DCPs, closed-caption files, posters, and some travel are included; a common rule of thumb is 3-5% of production budget for festival costs. Filmfestivalfever's programmer-author: 'at least $1K to test the waters, up to $10K' for saturation (~100+ submissions), which he does not endorse. Free or near-free top-tier entries (Short Movie Club's 2025 survey): Cannes official shorts selection, Clermont-Ferrand, Oberhausen, Zinebi, Mar del Plata, Cinema Jove — the FIAPF-accredited slate alone can be covered for $400-600. Scam filter: skip festivals under 3-5 years old, anything with 'FEEDBACK'/'Lift-Off' in the name, and anything that emails discount codes unsolicited. For an AFI-pedigree prestige short aiming at an awards push, the realistic planning number is 30-50 submissions / $2,500-4,000 in fees over 18 months, weighted early toward free-and-elite entries.

findings.topic: 3. FilmFreeway mechanics: waivers, discounts, and programmer relationships
findings.summary: Fee waivers are granted festival-by-festival, almost always by emailing the programmer with a screener link and a specific case; programmers verify the filmmaker's pedigree before granting. Many diversity-focused festivals (e.g., CAAMFest) formally offer need-based waivers, and FilmFreeway's Connecting Cultures Program gives underrepresented filmmakers a $500+ waiver package across 20+ partner festivals. The Film Festival Alliance is a trade org for festival ORGANIZERS, not filmmakers — its value to a filmmaker is vetting which festivals are legitimate.
findings.detail: Waiver mechanics (FilmFreeway's own Medium piece by festival founder Jon Gann, plus festival help pages): waivers exist mainly for solicited films and credible hardship cases; programmers 'find out the pedigree of the filmmakers, evaluate past projects, and look at the project under consideration' — so the ask should include a private screener, the AFI thesis pedigree, and a concrete reason (student-made, self-funded, underrepresented team). Verified examples of formal diversity/need waivers: CAAMFest grants discounted/waived fees case-by-case by email for demonstrated financial need; many identity-based festivals run the same policy informally — Black film festivals frequently waive for Black filmmakers on request (ask before paying, every time). FilmFreeway's Connecting Cultures Program awards the 'Tarkovski Grant': a submission-fee-waiver package worth at least $500 covering free entry to 20+ partner festivals, aimed at filmmakers underrepresented due to economic hardship, conflict, censorship, or limited access to international networks — a Nigerian director plausibly qualifies. Mechanically on FilmFreeway, waivers arrive as discount codes entered at checkout or as festival-issued 'free submission' invitations. [General knowledge, verify current terms — FilmFreeway blocks automated fetches: FilmFreeway Gold is a paid membership giving percentage discounts at thousands of participating festivals plus unlimited HD/4K hosting; student discounts are a standard checkout category at most US festivals and an AFI fellow/recent-grad qualifies at many.] Film Festival Alliance (filmfestivalalliance.org, verified): membership is festival organizers and exhibitors; offers best-practice standards, an accessibility scorecard, and a festival directory — use it as a legitimacy filter, not a submission channel. Programmer relationships remain the real fee-waiver engine: a film that wins early gets solicited (with waivers) by later festivals; track which programmers respond and keep them warm.

findings.topic: 4. The 18-24 month lifecycle: premiere → qualifying win → awards push → online release, and when to stop
findings.summary: The successful arc runs: 6-12 months chasing a top-tier world premiere; 6-12 more months cascading through Oscar-qualifying and identity-fit festivals hunting a qualifying WIN; an FYC push into the October-December Academy shorts voting window; then an online premiere with a curated partner. The Academy's rule since 2018 means a qualifying-festival win qualifies the short regardless of prior online release, and Vimeo's Staff Pick Premieres accept films within 24 months of playing in competition at an Oscar-qualifying event — those two clocks define when to stop.
findings.detail: Arc for a film picture-locked January 2026: (a) Months 0-9 (mid-2026 into early 2027): world-premiere attempts at the majors plus free elite entries (Clermont-Ferrand, Oberhausen). (b) Once the premiere lands: cascade into the ~180 festivals on the Academy's Short Film Qualifying Festival List, because the qualification route for a short is winning a designated qualifying award at a listed festival (or a qualifying theatrical run). Verified via Short of the Week's analysis of the July 2018 rule change: shorts 'are eligible for Oscar consideration if they win an Oscar-qualifying festival regardless of previous online distribution' — the win is what qualifies, so the campaign's center of gravity is qualifying WINS, not raw laurels. (c) Awards push: qualified shorts campaign through the fall shortlist/nomination voting of the target Oscar year (for this film realistically the 2028 ceremony cycle, entering by the Academy's fall 2027 deadlines — verify exact dates on oscars.org when the 100th/101st Awards rules post). (d) Online release: hold until the festival run has extracted its value, then premiere with a curator that brings an audience — Vimeo Staff Pick Premieres (verified eligibility: played in competition at an Oscar-qualifying event within the last 24 months; Vimeo adds editorial and marketing support), Short of the Week, or a genre/prestige channel. When to stop submitting — three converging clocks: (1) most festivals require completion within 18-24 months of the festival date, so a Jan-2026 film ages out of eligibility across late 2027-2028; (2) the Staff Pick Premieres 24-month window from the qualifying-event screening; (3) marginal economics — the filmfestivalfever guidance is to reassess after 6+ months of pure rejections, and standard advice is to wind down when acceptances plateau at festivals that add no programmer relationships, press, or qualifying potential. Typical total run: 12-18 months of active submissions, 18-24 months premiere-to-online.

findings.topic: 5. Grants and support for Black/African filmmakers' festival runs
findings.summary: Black Film Space is the most directly relevant verified source: its Emerging Filmmaker Grant explicitly allows funds for festival submissions, and membership ($75/yr) waives its application fees. Firelight Media's funds ($20K-50K unrestricted, incl. distribution) are documentary-only — a common misconception, so it does NOT fit this narrative short. ARRAY runs grants through ARRAY Alliance but is primarily a feature distributor; FilmFreeway's Connecting Cultures/Tarkovski Grant covers fees for underrepresented filmmakers.
findings.detail: Verified and usable: Black Film Space (blackfilmspace.com) — Emerging Filmmaker Grant ($3,000 in the 2025 cycle) whose funds 'may be used toward post-production, festival submissions, or distribution expenses'; principal photography complete by Sept 1, 2026 for the current cycle, so a completed 2026 thesis fits; $25 application fee, free for members ($75/yr); additional partner grants (Entertainmint $2,500; cliveRd proof-of-concept $10,000 in 2024) recur annually — watch blackfilmspace.com/bfsgrants. FilmFreeway Connecting Cultures Program — Tarkovski Grant: $500+ fee-waiver package to 20+ partner festivals for underrepresented filmmakers (see finding 3). Firelight Media — IMPORTANT caveat: Documentary Lab ($25K + mentorship), Firelight Fund ($20K-50K unrestricted incl. distribution), and Spark Fund are all restricted to NONFICTION filmmakers of color; a narrative short is ineligible, so don't spend a cycle applying. ARRAY (Ava DuVernay): ARRAY Releasing distributes features by Black filmmakers, women, and filmmakers of color, not shorts; ARRAY Alliance lists 'ARRAY Grants' for filmmaker funding — worth one email, but not a festival-fee pipeline (verified from arraynow.com; grant specifics not published on the fetched page). [General knowledge, labeled as such — verify current cycles before relying on them: The Black House Foundation supports Black filmmakers' presence at major festivals (Sundance and others) with community space and travel/lodging support once a film is selected; the HBO Short Film Award at the American Black Film Festival carries a ~$10,000 prize for Black-led narrative shorts; the DGA Student Film Awards include a category honoring African American student filmmakers and AFI films are eligible; many Black festivals — BlackStar, Pan African Film Festival, Martha's Vineyard AAFF, Urbanworld — are Oscar-qualifying for shorts and grant need-based waivers on request.] Web-search budget expired before these last items could be re-verified from official pages; treat bracketed items as leads to confirm, not booked facts.

findings.topic: 6. What AFI does institutionally for a thesis film — and what the team must do
findings.summary: AFI's verified institutional platforms are the AFI Conservatory Showcase at AFI FEST (thesis shorts screened with Variety as media partner in the 2020 edition), discipline Spotlights (Cinematography, Production Design — 2026 RSVP pages live), and a 501(c)(3) donation portal per thesis film. 'First Look' is USC's showcase, not AFI's — a correction to the question as posed. Nothing public documents AFI paying festival fees or running campaigns; the working assumption (labeled, verify with AFI's office) is that AFI holds rights as producer of record and the team drives and funds its own festival run under AFI clearance.
findings.detail: Verified from afi.com/conservatory.afi.com: (1) AFI Conservatory Showcase at AFI FEST — the 2020 edition screened 15 thesis narratives from the most recent graduating class, presented by Audi with Variety as media partner; AFI FEST itself is an Academy-qualifying festival, making the Showcase both an industry platform and a potential premiere venue (note: screening there spends world-premiere status, so the team must sequence it deliberately against Sundance/Cannes attempts). (2) Discipline showcases with 2026 RSVP pages already on the Conservatory sitemap: Cinematography Spotlight 2026 and Production Design Spotlight 2026, plus a Directing Showcase — for a chiaroscuro calling-card film, the Cinematography Spotlight is direct DP-and-director exposure to working professionals. (3) Thesis financing runs through AFI as a 501(c)(3): a public donation portal lists each year's thesis titles (23 films for 2025-26) for tax-deductible per-film gifts — this is how teams raise festival/finishing money without fiscal-sponsorship overhead. (4) Track record for pitching: AFI thesis films have earned 10 Academy Award nominations with 2 wins (Wikipedia), and the Conservatory claims 626 alumni films at Cannes/Berlin/Sundance/TIFF/Venice over five years. CORRECTION: 'First Look' is the USC School of Cinematic Arts' annual industry showcase (verified at cinema.usc.edu/firstlook — run by USC's Industry Relations Office with industry juries across six categories); AFI has no program by that name — its equivalents are the Conservatory Showcase + Spotlights. NOT publicly documented (verified absence on the Conservatory FAQ and site; labeled inference from general knowledge to confirm with AFI's festival/distribution office): AFI is producer of record and copyright holder on Conservatory films, festival submissions require AFI clearance and typically route through an AFI festivals/distribution contact, and AFI does not fund or run the festival campaign — the directing/producing team builds the strategy, fills the FilmFreeway project, requests waivers, and pays fees from the thesis budget or their own fundraising. Action item for the team: email the Conservatory's festival office for (a) the clearance procedure, (b) any standing festival-fee support or waiver relationships, and (c) the DCP/deliverables package AFI provides.

findings.topic: EXTRA A. Student Academy Awards and student-track competitions are a second qualifying lane
findings.summary: As an AFI thesis film, Killer of Men likely has a student-competition lane the general playbook ignores: the Student Academy Awards (whose medal winners become eligible for Oscar consideration) plus BAFTA Student Awards and the DGA Student Film Awards. These are high-prestige, low-cost entries that do not depend on festival premieres.
findings.detail: [Labeled general knowledge — oscars.org blocked automated fetch and the search budget was exhausted; verify eligibility windows on oscars.org/saa before planning.] The Student Academy Awards accept films made within a course of study at an accredited institution, with entry deadlines historically falling in late spring (May-June) each year — estimated from prior cycles, not confirmed for 2027. Medal-winning films become eligible to compete for the Academy Award in the corresponding shorts category, i.e., an SAA win is itself a qualification path that bypasses the festival-win requirement. For a film picture-locked January 2026 by fellows graduating in 2026, the relevant cycle is likely 2026 (possibly already closed) or 2027 depending on completion-date rules — this is a verify-immediately item because missing the window forfeits the lane. Adjacent student lanes worth confirming: BAFTA Student Awards, and the DGA Student Film Awards which include an award recognizing African American student filmmakers. AFI films have historically competed in all of these.

findings.topic: EXTRA B. Strategic implications specific to this film's profile
findings.summary: Three campaign implications fall out of the research: front-load the free elite European entries (Clermont-Ferrand is the world's biggest shorts market and free), treat Berlinale as the only major where prior screenings genuinely kill eligibility, and budget the Black-festival circuit as a near-zero-fee lane via waiver requests — while sequencing AFI FEST's Conservatory Showcase so it doesn't accidentally spend the world premiere.
findings.detail: (1) Free top-tier entries verified by Short Movie Club: Cannes shorts selection, Clermont-Ferrand, Oberhausen, Zinebi, Cinema Jove — for a tenebrist period piece with festival-friendly craft, these cost nothing but premiere status, so they belong in Wave 1 alongside Sundance/SXSW/Tribeca/TIFF. (2) Eligibility asymmetry (Short of the Week, verified): Sundance shorts ignore prior screenings AND online release; Berlinale Shorts and DOK Leipzig are the strict ones — so if Berlinale is a genuine target (Nigerian diaspora themes play well there), it must come before any public screening including the AFI Showcase; if it is not, the premiere-hold discipline can relax after the first top-tier landing. (3) The film's identity fit — Black American history, Yoruba spirituality, Nigerian director — maps onto a circuit (BlackStar, Pan African FF, ABFF, Urbanworld, Martha's Vineyard AAFF, plus African festivals like AFRIFF/Durban) where several are Oscar-qualifying and most grant need-based or student waivers on a direct email; budget these at near-zero fees but real travel costs, which is exactly what Black House-style travel support and Black Film Space grant funds can absorb. (4) The single most time-sensitive verification for the parent agent: whether AFI has already scheduled this film into a 2026 Conservatory Showcase/AFI FEST slot, since that decision constrains every top-tier premiere submission this fall.
